body.en: HL Statistics & Probability establishes formal measure-theoretic foundations for continuous random variables, calculus of expectation and variance, Poisson processes, linear combinations of independent normals, and Bessel-corrected unbiased estimators.

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Probability Axioms, Law of Total Probability & Bayes

body.en:
Kolmogorov Axioms & Conditional Probability: For events in sample space \(S\): \[ 0 \le P(A) \le 1, \quad P(S) = 1, \quad P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B). \] Conditional probability of event \(A\) given \(B\) (with \(P(B) > 0\)): \[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}. \] Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if and only if \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B) \iff P(A \mid B) = P(A)\).

Law of Total Probability & Bayes' Theorem: Let \(\{B_1, B_2, \dots, B_k\}\) be a partition of \(S\) (mutually exclusive and exhaustive events with \(P(B_i) > 0\)):

  • Law of Total Probability: \[ P(A) = \sum_{i=1}^k P(A \cap B_i) = \sum_{i=1}^k P(A \mid B_i)P(B_i). \]
  • Bayes' Theorem: Evaluates posterior probabilities updated from prior evidence: \[ P(B_j \mid A) = \frac{P(A \mid B_j)P(B_j)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(A \mid B_j)P(B_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^k P(A \mid B_i)P(B_i)}. \]

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Tools — Poisson Distribution & Linear Combinations

body.en:
The Poisson Distribution: Models the count of rare events occurring in a fixed interval of continuous time or space. A random variable \(X \sim \text{Po}(\lambda)\) (with parameter \(\lambda > 0\)) assumes:

  1. Events occur independently.
  2. Events occur at a constant average rate \(\lambda\).
  3. Events occur singly (two events cannot occur simultaneously).

Probability Mass Function (PMF): \[ P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots \] Theoretical Moments: Mean and variance are identically equal: \[ E[X] = \lambda, \quad \text{Var}(X) = \lambda. \] Sum of Independent Poissons: If \(X_1 \sim \text{Po}(\lambda_1)\) and \(X_2 \sim \text{Po}(\lambda_2)\) are independent, then: \[ X_1 + X_2 \sim \text{Po}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2). \]

Linear Combinations of Random Variables: For any random variables \(X, Y\) and constants \(a, b\):

  • Expectation (Always Linear): \(E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]\).
  • Variance of Independent Variables: If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent: \[ \text{Var}(aX \pm bY) = a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y). \]
  • Linear Combinations of Independent Normal Variables: If \(X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)\) and \(Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)\) are independent, then \(W = aX + bY\) is strictly normally distributed: \[ W = aX + bY \sim N(a\mu_X + b\mu_Y, \; a^2\sigma_X^2 + b^2\sigma_Y^2). \] In particular, the difference \(D = X - Y \sim N(\mu_X - \mu_Y, \; \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2)\) (variances always add!).

note.en: For a Poisson distribution, the mean and variance are always identical: \(E(X)\) = Var(\(X\)) = \(\lambda\). The mode (peak bar) occurs at ⌊\(\lambda\)⌋. When \(\lambda\) is small the distribution is right-skewed; as \(\lambda\) increases it becomes bell-shaped, approaching a normal distribution with mean \(\lambda\) and variance \(\lambda\).

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem: Continuous Random Variables & Estimator Unbiasedness

body.en:
Continuous Random Variables & Calculus of Probability: Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with probability density function (PDF) \(f(x)\):

  • Density Criteria: \(f(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), and \[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,dx = 1. \]
  • Interval Probability & Single-Point Nullity: For any \(a < b\), \(P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). For any specific real point \(c\), \(P(X = c) = \int_c^c f(x)\,dx = 0\).
  • Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF): Defined by \(F(x) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt\). By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \[ \frac{d}{dx}F(x) = f(x) \quad \text{at all continuity points of } f. \]
  • Expectation & Higher Moments: \[ E[X] = \mu = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x f(x)\,dx, \quad E[X^2] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^2 f(x)\,dx, \quad \text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2. \]
  • Median & Mode: The median \(m\) is the root of \(F(m) = \int_{-\infty}^m f(x)\,dx = 0.5\). The mode is the value of \(x\) where \(f(x)\) attains its global maximum.

Sampling Theory & Proof of Bessel's Correction: Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) be an i.i.d. sample from a population with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\):

  • Sample Mean Unbiasedness: \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i\). Then \(E[\bar{X}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum E[X_i] = \frac{1}{n}(n\mu) = \mu\). Standard error \(\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\).
  • Sample Variance Unbiasedness (Bessel's Correction): If we used the naive sample variance \(S_n^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\), its expectation is: \[ E[S_n^2] = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2 \neq \sigma^2 \quad (\text{downwardly biased!}). \] Proof: Write \(X_i - \bar{X} = (X_i - \mu) - (\bar{X} - \mu)\). Summing squares: \[ \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 - n(\bar{X} - \mu)^2. \] Taking expectations: \(E\left[\sum (X_i - \mu)^2\right] = n\sigma^2\) and \(E[n(\bar{X} - \mu)^2] = n\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = n\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) = \sigma^2\). Thus: \[ E\left[\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\right] = n\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 = (n-1)\sigma^2. \] Dividing by \(n - 1\) yields the unbiased estimator \(S_{n-1}^2\): \[ S_{n-1}^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2 \implies E[S_{n-1}^2] = \sigma^2. \quad \blacksquare \]

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Statistics & Probability (HL))

body.en:
Why Variance Scales as \(a^2\) and Independent Variances Always Add: By definition, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \mu_Y)^2]\). For \(Y = aX - bW\) with independent \(X, W\), subtracting its mean \(\mu_Y = a\mu_X - b\mu_W\) gives:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[(a(X - \mu_X) - b(W - \mu_W))^2\right] = a^2\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)^2] - 2ab\,\operatorname{Cov}(X,W) + b^2\mathbb{E}[(W-\mu_W)^2] \]

Because independence implies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, W) = 0\), the cross term vanishes and \((-b)^2 = +b^2\), proving \(\operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(W)\). Uncertainty compounds whether random variables are added or subtracted.

label.en: Worked Example 4.1 — Continuous Random Variable Calculus

problem.en: A continuous random variable \(X\) has PDF \(f(x) = kx(2 - x)\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\) and \(f(x) = 0\) elsewhere. Find: (a) the constant \(k\); (b) the median \(m\); (c) the variance \(\text{Var}(X)\).

solution.en:
(a) Normalization condition:
\[ \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx = 1 \implies k \int_0^2 (2x - x^2)\,dx = 1 \] \[ k \left[ x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^2 = k\left( 4 - \frac{8}{3} \right) = k\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) = 1 \implies k = \frac{3}{4}. \]

(b) Find the median \(m\):
By symmetry about \(x = 1\), the median is \(m = 1\). We can confirm by integrating: \[ \int_0^1 \frac{3}{4}(2x - x^2)\,dx = \frac{3}{4}\left[ x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^1 = \frac{3}{4}\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}. \quad \checkmark \] Thus the median is \(m = 1\).

(c) Find \(\text{Var}(X)\):
By symmetry, \(E[X] = 1\). Compute \(E[X^2]\): \[ E[X^2] = \int_0^2 x^2 f(x)\,dx = \frac{3}{4}\int_0^2 (2x^3 - x^4)\,dx = \frac{3}{4}\left[ \frac{2x^4}{4} - \frac{x^5}{5} \right]_0^2 = \frac{3}{4}\left( 8 - \frac{32}{5} \right) = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{8}{5}\right) = \frac{6}{5}. \] Then: \[ \text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \frac{6}{5} - 1^2 = \frac{1}{5} = 0.2. \]

label.en: Worked Example 4.2 — Poisson Rate Scaling & Conditional Probability

problem.en: Incoming inquiries to an advisory hotline follow a Poisson distribution with an average rate of 4 per 10-minute window. Find: (a) the probability of exactly 6 inquiries in a 20-minute window; (b) given that at least 2 inquiries arrived in a 10-minute window, find the probability that exactly 3 inquiries arrived.

solution.en:
(a) 20-minute window:
The rate scales linearly with the interval length: \(\lambda_{20} = 4 \times 2 = 8\). Let \(Y \sim \text{Po}(8)\): \[ P(Y = 6) = \frac{e^{-8} \cdot 8^6}{6!} = \frac{e^{-8} \cdot 262144}{720} \approx 0.1221. \]

(b) Conditional probability in 10-minute window (\(X \sim \text{Po}(4)\)):
We need \(P(X = 3 \mid X \ge 2) = \dfrac{P(X = 3)}{P(X \ge 2)}\).
Compute \(P(X \ge 2)\): \[ P(X \ge 2) = 1 - P(X = 0) - P(X = 1) = 1 - e^{-4}\left(1 + 4\right) = 1 - 5e^{-4} \approx 1 - 0.09158 = 0.90842. \] Compute \(P(X = 3)\): \[ P(X = 3) = \frac{e^{-4} \cdot 4^3}{3!} = \frac{64 e^{-4}}{6} = \frac{32}{3}e^{-4} \approx 0.19537. \] Therefore: \[ P(X = 3 \mid X \ge 2) = \frac{0.19537}{0.90842} \approx 0.215. \]

label.en: Worked Example 4.3 — Difference of Independent Normal Distributions

problem.en: The weights of chocolate bars from Brand A and Brand B are independently distributed as \(A \sim N(100, 16)\) and \(B \sim N(95, 9)\) (in grams). Find the probability that a randomly selected bar of Brand A weighs more than a randomly selected bar of Brand B by at least 8 grams.

solution.en:
1. Define the difference random variable \(D = A - B\).

2. Since \(A\) and \(B\) are independent normal variables, \(D\) is also normally distributed:
Mean: \(\mu_D = E[A - B] = E[A] - E[B] = 100 - 95 = 5\).
Variance: \(\sigma_D^2 = \text{Var}(A - B) = 1^2\text{Var}(A) + (-1)^2\text{Var}(B) = 16 + 9 = 25\).
Thus \(\sigma_D = \sqrt{25} = 5\), and \(D \sim N(5, 25)\).

3. We require \(P(D \ge 8)\):
Standardize: \[ z = \frac{8 - \mu_D}{\sigma_D} = \frac{8 - 5}{5} = 0.6. \] Using the standard normal distribution: \[ P(D \ge 8) = P(Z \ge 0.6) = 1 - \Phi(0.6) \approx 1 - 0.7257 = 0.2743. \]

label.en: ⚠ Topic 4 Exam Traps: Poisson Scaling, Variances & Unbiased Estimators

body.en:
Poisson Rate Scaling: If events arrive at rate \(\lambda\) per minute, in \(t\) minutes the rate is \(\lambda t\). You must scale \(\lambda\) directly before calculating probabilities.

Variance of a Difference: For independent variables, \(\text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)\). A rampant error is subtracting variances: \(\text{Var}(X) - \text{Var}(Y)\). Variability always compounds!

\(2X\) vs \(X_1 + X_2\): \(\text{Var}(2X) = 2^2\text{Var}(X) = 4\sigma^2\), whereas \(\text{Var}(X_1 + X_2) = \text{Var}(X_1) + \text{Var}(X_2) = 2\sigma^2\). The sum of two independently chosen items has half the variance of doubling a single selected item.

Worked Example (AA HL Paper 1 — 8 marks):
A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x) = kx(2 - x)$ for $0 \le x \le 2$, and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise.
(a) Show that $k = \frac{3}{4}$. [3]
(b) Find $\text{E}(X)$ and $\text{Var}(X)$. [5]

Official IB Markscheme Solution:
(a) Total probability $= 1$: $\int_0^2 k(2x - x^2)\,dx = 1 \implies k\left[x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 1$ [M1] [A1]
$k\left(4 - \frac{8}{3}\right) = \frac{4}{3}k = 1 \implies k = \frac{3}{4}$ [A1] [AG]
(b) By symmetry of $f(x) = \frac{3}{4}x(2-x)$ about $x = 1$ (or integration), $\text{E}(X) = 1$ [A1]
$\text{E}(X^2) = \frac{3}{4}\int_0^2 (2x^3 - x^4)\,dx = \frac{3}{4}\left[\frac{x^4}{2} - \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2 = \frac{3}{4}\left(8 - \frac{32}{5}\right) = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{8}{5}\right) = \frac{6}{5}$ [M1] [A1]
$\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^2) - [\text{E}(X)]^2 = \frac{6}{5} - 1^2 = \frac{1}{5} = 0.2$ [M1] [A1]

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Statistics & Probability (HL))

rows.en: Produces smaller or even negative variance for the difference of independent variables.
Always add variances of independent variables: \(\sigma_{X-Y}^2 = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2\).
Confuses the variance of the sample mean \(\sigma^2/n\) with its standard error.
Absence of sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\) is true.
Write in context: "There is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha\) level to reject \(H_0\)."

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Statistics & Probability (HL)

body.en: Exam Marking Tip (IB Diploma Mathematics: AA / AI Higher Level (Papers 1, 2 & 3)): Always state the distribution parameters explicitly (e.g., \(X \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) or \(\bar{X} \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\)) and sketch a quick shaded bell curve before standardizing to \(z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\). This secures the method mark even if a rounding slip occurs later.

question.en: A continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = 2e^{-2x}\) for \(x \ge 0\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Find the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\) and determine the exact median of \(X\).

solution.en: 1. Find CDF for \(x \ge 0\): \[ F(x) = \int_0^x 2e^{-2t}\,dt = \left[ -e^{-2t} \right]_0^x = 1 - e^{-2x}. \] 2. Set \(F(m) = 0.5\) to find the median \(m\): \[ 1 - e^{-2m} = 0.5 \implies e^{-2m} = 0.5 \implies -2m = \ln(0.5) = -\ln 2 \implies m = \frac{\ln 2}{2}. \]
